speechtext: We have discussed before the possibilities of donations having been made to the Red Cross and thence to housing corporations, because the service clubs themselves are not treated as charitable organizations-
They are not profit-making organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All right, that is the distinction. So that if a service club embarked upon a scheme of building houses of this kind we would have to take a look at them to see if they conformed to what we think is the very remote possibility of income in the future.
They would have to come to you before starting to build and get your ideas as to whether or not they would be exempt?

For instance, if the Canadian Legion were putting up such housing.

I have a question which I think may have been answered at least in part by

the last reply of the minister. However, I would like to be perfectly clear that I understand correctly that he has said this exemption is not to apply necessarily only to agencies set up by municipal corporations. The minister will recall last year we had some discussion about the various agencies and their building developments in British Columbia and the specific question I would like to ask now is this: If organizations are set up, as are now found in British Columbia, under the societies act, for the specific purposes set out in the section, even though they are not an official agency of a municipal corporation, could the donations to such an organization qualify for exemption provided the manner in which the organization is conducting its affairs meets with the general conditions as laid down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Paragraph 10. If there are no questions then, proceed to paragraph 11.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution in this paragraph to my way of thinking is the most important of the resolutions with which we have been dealing under the Income Tax Act. I would indeed be unmannerly if I failed to recognize its virtue after having asked for it in each of the four sessions of parliament during which it has been my privilege to be here. This could affect some 400,000 taxpayers who are self-employed; in fact it could go beyond that as framed because it is open to the employees who are not already contributors to an approved pension fund.
I recall that my first plea on behalf of the self-employed described them as being discriminated against by the legislation as it stood in May of 1953 when Mr. Abbott was finance minister. Again in each subsequent year I spoke on this question, as did many other members of the house. I further believe representations have been made to the government, perhaps over a period of ten years, by different associations of self-employed persons, who find themselves in the invidious position of not being able to save for their retirement money which had not been taxed as would have been the case had they been contributing to approved plans.
I do not propose to labour the point but this provision seems to be relatively simple and I compliment the department on devising a scheme of such simplicity to meet this problem. I recall that Mr. Abbott said in 1953 on page 3704 of Hansard, after an argument was over: "I have not taken a final position but the difficulties-the inequities- still appal me." He then listed in the course of his address some eight or nine reasons which appealed to him as good reasons for not

proceeding, one of which was the technical and practical difficulty of finding a means for devising the machinery by which the selfemployed could be given the advantages enjoyed by those in employment for others.
As I recall it in each year since then, the present minister has made that his only reason for not acting at the particular time.
I say now that when this scheme is presented to us with this relatively simple and clear program of annuities and of trust funds for the provision of retirement annuities it appears to me that the reason why we have had to wait was something other than the difficulty of devising the machinery for putting this policy into effect. It is not necessary to suggest what the reason may be for the appearance of this in the budget this year, because, as I say, it does affect a large number of people and is likely to commend itself to them. Moreover, this is a very opportune time at which to bring it in.
In concluding my remarks, and expressing my gratification at what is now being done, I do not wish to detract from the appreciation I have extended to the minister except to this extent: that it is too late, and that it is obviously designed for a purpose which I expect to expose in the course of the next two months.

Mr. Chairman, this interesting provision will be to the advantage of possibly, I understand, half a million Canadians, mainly professional and business people. It will, I think, give those people a measure of fair play which has been denied to them in the past, and as one who has sat here and heard the former minister of finance state the many reasons why such a plan could not be adopted, and announce all the difficulties in connection with carrying through such action, I can only say that the government moves in a mysterious way its wonders to perform.
Anyway I do hope that this recognition of the need to be fair in this respect to half a million or more Canadians indicates that the [DOT] minister is beginning to think in terms of the benefit which would be derived by all Canadians from a national industrial pension scheme. I have spoken on this subject at some length in the past. I am going to be quite brief now, but I cannot resist bringing the wishes of my constituents and the policy of this group once more to the attention of the minister, because we feel that such a scheme is necessary if industrial workers are to have a measure of security on retirement, and the mobility which is their right in a modern democratic civilization so that that they may move from one company to another and not be chained to one area;
Income Tax Act
in other words, the right to the full security that would be provided by such a national scheme.
I think that in view of the large public investment in pension schemes-and a much greater investment still will result from the present changes in the Income Tax Act- the government has a direct responsibility for taking some action with respect to a national industrial pension scheme in this country. I recall that last year we were told that over $30 million was lost to the federal treasury owing to pension schemes, and that sum will probably increase rapidly in the future. Future contributions, deductions and so on will make for even faster growth than in the past and I think that the present occasion is a splendid opportunity for the minister, in the words of Winston Churchill, to "bring the magic of the law of averages to the rescue of millions who need it at this time."
I do urge that this matter be given immediate consideration, and that it be referred to the committee on industrial relations for study during the course of the next parliament; and I am one who trusts I will be back here to hear the minister make such an announcement.
Before resuming my seat I will draw to the minister's attention the fact that some days ago the Minister of National Revenue, in reply to a question I had asked, said that a committee of his department was studying and revising the booklet that contains the rules with respect to registered pension plans. I do urge that he should give consideration to the representations made by various labour organizations in this country and hon. members on both sides of the house, and make sure that pension vesting rights are maintained under the rules, and that provision is made to enforce the regulations.
The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Trail, British Columbia recognizes its responsibility as a company in this respect, and has given its employees a letter which, in effect, guarantees vesting rights. This was done during the last negotiations with the union for the contract. I urge that pending introduction by the minister of a national industrial pension scheme he should provide this greater security to all industrial workers in Canada by enforcing the law on a national scale, and by enforcing provisions which at the present time are given to its employees by one farsighted company in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want the hon. member for Kootenay West to take it from me that we accept the thesis that we have the responsibility for seeing that there is such a plan, because in saying that one

On the other hand, there is no question at all in my mind but that stability of income and security for the future do work out to the advantage of the taxpayers of Canada generally, because such security minimizes the number of occasions on which emergency measures might have to be taken here in order to look after persons who otherwise might have been able to look after themselves through the kind of pension program the hon. member has in mind.
I merely say this to indicate that the Minister of Finance is not disinterested about seeing that adequate security and income is provided at all times.
May I turn for a moment to the hon. member for St. Paul's, only to say this: that he was so kindly in his reference to the progress the government has made that I anticipate that as he goes about during the next two months he will say that I brought this legislation before the house solely because of the impending events of the next two months. I will also follow him about and say I am sure he has been an upright and just statesman in recommending this course for the last four years and that at no time did he have in mind the events of the next two months.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to make one or two comments about this. I am going to flatter the minister by reading a paragraph from his own speech at page 2225 of Hansard. My point is that I want to ask the minister to tell us, if he can and will, whether there is any principle at work behind these customs changes or whether it is a matter of just plugging a hole here and there. I want to read briefly from the minister's speech in which he says:
Since my last budget there has been a new and important development in the field of international tariff arrangements.
And then he said:
This month. I understand, six leading countries on the continent of Europe are signing an agreement to recast their tariff and trade policies.
I was a little surprised by those words "I understand". I suppose he was merely playing the thing down because the minister, of all people, should have had accurate and up

to the minute information about what was taking place. If he had not, I would have had grave doubts about his competency for his job, but I know he did know all about that and that this was just a manner of speaking.
And then he went on to say:
Canadian trade will undoubtedly be affected by these developments. It is too early to forecast what the effects may be. The government is. however, following these events with very active interest through our diplomatic and trade missions-
And by other means. The minister reminds us that we are one of the contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade and of the organization for European economic co-operation, and that we are also keeping in close touch with other commonwealth countries.
I hope the minister will say a few words about this. I think that tariffs, from which we have been happily free for so long, may not be content to remain as far in the background as they have. I just happened across a speech delivered by an American congressman from West Virginia in the publication Vital Speeches for February 15, and without reading from it at any length I will just give the committee the tenor of what he had to say. He said that congress alone has the power to regulate foreign commerce. He is very suspicious of the action taken by the executive under powers given by congress and in the course of his speech he remarks that he is very much against having anything to do with the International Trade Organization and so on. I need not take the time of the committee to read this. He complains that the state department, in spite of the warning they have had from congress, has not relinquished its goal which, I take it, he believes is to try to do something to liberalize trade. As I have said,-and as has often been said before in this house-we have every reason to believe that just as soon as the United States regards itself as being pinched in any way, we may And them taking strong tariff action against us.
That brings us back to the European situation. I wish the minister would say a word on that matter. In a publication I have here entitled, "The Department of State Bulletin" the United States have pious hopes to express about the European movement to which the minister has referred. They say:
.	.	. It is our hope and expectation that the
negotiations on the common market and free trade area will be carried forward and concluded in such a manner that from these European initiatives will come a new contribution to the unity and prosperity of Europe and the Atlantic community and to the welfare of the entire free world.
When I say they are pious sentiments, I do not want to say it in a cynical way. I think those are the real sentiments of the United States administration. But as we

know, they are at the opposite extreme. Here the executive has all power and there the executive sometimes has very little power. If we could only find a half-way house whereby the executive could have enough power but not too much here and the legislative could have enough power but not too much there, we should be in a happier position in both cases.
But the other point I wish to make is this. As we have said on other occasions, and as I wish to say again, I think we are constantly disappointed, in spite of the comfortable references made, in the fact that the government does not seem to be wholehearted or even halfhearted in pursuing to the utmost the possibilities which though not illimitable are not insubstantial in the way of commonwealth trade. I realize that for a government that is, shall we say, almost inebriated with surpluses and easy money these last many months, which has been seeing a boom at work, it is hard perhaps to take these questions as seriously as we should. Particularly with this situation in Europe facing us, I believe it could become a very serious matter. I think it is at least a significant matter. I hope that the minister may have a few remarks to make to us about our trade situation and about the considerations which he had in mind in recommending the tariff changes which he is recommending.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is, of course, a matter that should have been covered in the budget debate itself and on which I had thought to say something the other night. However, I do not think it would be proper to make any extended remarks at all at this time about tariff matters generally at the resolution stage preceding a bill. However, I note what my hon. friend has said. I want to point out to him that perhaps he cannot be satisfied no matter what the conditions may be. The executive in the United States has much greater power for making tariff changes than have we in the sense that the executive may do certain things by executive order with or without the consent of congress at that particular time whereas we are obliged to come forward once a year and submit tariff changes at that time and seek the approval of parliament for them, though we make them effective when they are announced.
With respect to the situation in Europe, I was not either uninformed or intentionally vague in my use of the words "I understand". Rather I used them out of not an abundance of caution but merely out of proper caution, I think, because the date for supposed signing of the agreement was still some ten days ahead and I knew that the parties concerned
Customs Tariff
were still negotiating. All we had was a date on which it was expected that certain agreements would be reached. We were not, of course, parties to the agreement. We were fully informed about the progress of the negotiation through the organizations of the general agreement on tariffs and trade but not to the extent that we could have influenced the result because we did not feel at that time that representations ought to be made since it was a purely domestic matter with the six nations concerned.
On the other hand, to say that we were indifferent to the result would be far from the truth because this is perhaps the beginning of a much larger movement which will end with a much greater agreement with respect to tariffs and trade within the western world. I am quite sure that all of us would hope that the results of these agreements would be freer rather than more restricted exchange of goods and that in the remote sense there could not be the restricted results which have led in the past to serious friction between nations. On the other hand we also hope that the result of this agreement that is presently made and those that might be made in the future would result in more profit for the persons concerned because a prosperous nation is less likely to be subject to the pressures which would result in envy of what the neighbour might have.
On that latter point may I say that I think the time is coming in the not too distant future when there will have to be discussions with respect to the free trade area, if I may use that phrase for lack of a better description, in western Europe. There is no question at all that the Canadian government is vitally interested in the results which might ensue from those negotiations. We have been informed about them and have been studying the consequences to Canadian trade in some detail for several months. When the matter has reached a point where more direct consultations are being held we shall, of course, have our say not only within GATT but no doubt through other more direct methods. My understanding is that there will be just a preliminary meeting of GATT for the purpose of preparing for the negotiations leading to the extension of the present agreements as of July 1 next year and that there will be fairly extensive tariff discussions beginning in late September or October and running no doubt throughout the whole of the winter.
We as formerly firmly believe that these agreements have been to the great advantage of Canada, not only to the government, in the sense that they have kept the tariff out of our problems from day to day, but indeed

Customs Tariff
in the maintenance of trading relations on an even keel so that traders, exporters and importers particularly, may have fairly firm ideas not only from day to day but for months ahead as to what costs they might have to bear in order to carry out the trade they have in mind. I assure my hon. friend that we will hope to continue the present agreements with whatever changes circumstances may require, as we see them and as our co-signers may feel are warranted and that in the discussion on the other matter- that is the western European approach to a freer trade area-we shall do what we can to preserve our present trading arrangements and our outlet for Canadian goods while seeking to extend them of course under proper terms that might be called for by those with whom we are obliged to negotiate. I do not feel that I should go further than that at the moment.
I want to say one other thing about this resolution, if my hon. friend will forgive me. I should like the committee to understand that I may find it necessary to undertake amendments to the customs tariff bill at a later time during this session. I would suggest that if we find it possible we should pass the resolution now so the bill could be printed and circulated in the normal way, and that I be permitted unanimous consent at that time to move amendments rather than having to table resolutions which would precede that. This would be in the interest of saving time. I think if I find I have to do that, when the time comes I will probably get fairly widespread support for what I have in mind. I would not want to give notice now as to what the particular item might be.

Locomotives and railway passenger, baggage and freight cars, being the property or under the control of railway companies in the United States, running upon any line or road crossing the frontier, so long as Canadian locomotives and cars are admitted free under similar circumstances into the United States, under regulations prescribed by the minister:	Mostfavoured-nation tariff, free; general tariff, free.

Excise Act

Mr. Chairman, when we were on another item a few minutes ago the parliamentary assistant said he would deal with it when we came to the Excise Act. I think he quoted a figure of some $60,000 odd. Was that the revenue collected by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

Well, Mr. Chairman, I would like to have this straight in my mind. Is this a duty imposed on tobacco that is sold by the farmer to the packer? When it is sold to the packer who puts on an excise stamp for resale when it is to be resold by the packer?

speechtext:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act and to provide:
1. That in determining the aggregate net value of property subject to duty under the Dominion Succession Duty Act upon the death, after the 31st

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Dominion Succession Duty Act day of March, 1957, of a predecessor, there shall be deducted the dutiable value of any succession to a charitable organization in Canada operated exclusively as such and not for the benefit, gain or profit of any person, member or shareholder thereof.
2. That where provincial duties have been paid in respect of property subject to duty under the Dominion Succession Duty Act upon the death, after the 31st day of March, 1957, of a predecessor, the successor to that property may deduct from the duty otherwise payable under the Dominion Succession Duty Act in respect of that propertv, one-half of the duty otherwise so payable in respect thereof.

Mr. Chairman, under the succession duty act an estate under $50,000 is free from tax but if it should be $50,001 the whole thing then becomes taxable. Now would it not be wise-and I know the minister has had a lot of correspondence on this subject and many organizations have asked him questions to the same effect-if the government would allow the first $50,000 of any estate to be free of tax and then, after that, to be treated in the same way as it is at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I indicated in my budget speech, a revision of the succession duty act will be ready, I hope, in the fall. It can be taken for granted that it will be ready at that time.
I hope that provision will be considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is a simple question and the simple answer is that if you did that you would have to either reduce your revenue by so many millions of dollars or you would have to increase the rate so as to retain your present revenue. It is just a question of how much money you want to take out of this tax, whether you leave it at the original exemption or do as my hon. friend suggests. If we are to get the $60 million or $70 million that we expect to get in the coming year we must leave the present rates to take care of that or to make it, as my hon. friend suggests, a real exemption with the tax rate starting higher.

Does not the minister feel that some of the first $50,000 should be exempt? Take for instance an estate of $45,000, the government inspectors would come around and revalue it, and before you know it you are over $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But the tax would never reduce the estate below $50,000.

I would like to follow up something which my hon. friend the member for Peterborough said. I have had a large

number of letters on this question because I happen to represent a riding where there are a great many very active and intelligent women who work in organizations and they very frequently put their problems in my lap, collectively and individually. I do suggest that there is some merit in their argument, although I can appreciate the argument of the minister today in answer to my hon. friend's question. However, I think there could be a fairer way of applying succession duty tax with a very little reduction in the revenue to the exchequer and I do urge the minister to give consideration to these representations from women and from women's organizations who feel that they have a definite grievance in the present circumstances and conditions.

But when this act was put in the dollar was worth a great deal more than it is today. The dollar is worth only about 50 cents today, or at least it only buys about 50 per cent of what it would have bought in 1940. This makes a great deal of difference to a person who is left with a small estate of say $60,000 and who has to pay tax on the whole works.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could give us a calculation with respect to a particular estate. I am sure all the hon. members have had representations of this sort; could the minister give us what would be the difference in the revenue to the treasury on an estate of $100,000 if the succession duty tax were changed so that there would be $50,000 deductible. Some of the representations I have had were to the effect that there should be an extra $25,000. Perhaps the minister could give us a rough estimate of the difference this would make in loss of revenue, if this recommendation were to be adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would rather that the resolution were passed and I will answer that question on the bill.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Kootenay West I have received a good many representations from these women's organizations throughout my riding and they have been unanimous in the request that the $50,000 be a true exemption for the purpose of the act. They have, however, gone a lot further and in this regard I think they have made a pretty logical request, which is to the effect that half of the estate be considered as having been earned and accumulated by the wife.

It has been pointed out in other debates, during this session particularly, that in the case of a farm wife she has worked equally as hard as the man in building up the estate and the farm. She has milked the cows and fed the chickens and been up early in the morning. I feel that these women, particularly on the farms-although this is also applicable to almost any other case; and indeed how many of us would get anywhere without our wives -for the purpose of this act should be considered as having earned and accumulated these moneys. Therefore there would be no succession duty chargeable on this amount of $50,000.

I had intended to reproach the minister for the delay in dealing with succession duty but he has really drawn my fire by explaining that work is now going forward steadily. Of course I do hope he will not have the burden of making the decisions himself later in the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am in complete agreement but from a different standpoint.

I do want to make a suggestion, however. I fully realize what the minister says to the effect that the money has to come from somewhere, but it would seem to be fairer not to have this arbitrary throwback of the $50,000 into the tax field but rather whatever increase in rate is necessary. That it would be far preferable to having this benefit suddenly taken away by reason of having $1 over the $50,000.

It seems to me that the minister should take into more careful consideration the proposals that have been made. In view of the decreased value of the dollar during the last few years it does seem to me that it would be only fair to what might be termed reasonably small estates because after all an estate of $50,000 today is nothing like as large an estate as it was a few years ago. The value of the dollar comes into the picture and while the minister says that he would have to increase the rates on the larger estates, it does seem to me that it would be only fair in relation to these other estates-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I didn't say that.

Oh, well I understood you to say that you would have to increase the rates accordingly, all along the line if you gave the exemption up to $50,000. Perhaps I didn't get it right, but was it only on the large estates that you would increase the rates, or
Dominion Succession Duty Act would you increase the rates on all if you wanted to maintain the same rate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The same aggregate collection.

Yes. I am speaking of the size of the surplus you have. I don't know why you need to increase that at all, and when a more economical government is here in October it might not be considered necessary to maintain the rates which apply now.
But let that be as it may, I do feel that it would be only fair to extend this limit of $50,000. If a limit of $50,000 was right a few years ago, it is not right now, and, after all if it is extended and if it is necessary, as has been suggested, to increase the rate in order to maintain the present level of revenue, then it would be much easier and cause less hardship to our people if the increase were applied to the larger estates. I hope the minister will give some consideration to this. As the hon. member for Peterborough has said, to have an estate which just goes one dollar over the $50,000, and then to take the whole $50,000

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But the levy is only on a dollar. No amount of tax will reduce the estate below the $50,000.
The excess is taxed; if it is $60,000, the $10,000 is taxed.

Even so, in relation to the value of the dollar it seems to me it should be paid on a basis which is in relation to the decreased value of our dollar, which I am not prepared at the moment to define exactly, but I think a reasonable figure would be $65,000 or $70,000. The value of the dollar has been decreasing steadily in purchasing power. Someone has mentioned $75,000 and it appears to me that $75,000 would be a reasonable amount. If we were right about the figure we fixed before, we are certainly wrong now; and if we are correct now we were certainly wrong at that time, and I submit that the minister should seriously consider such an amendment as has been suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are giving consideration to all these matters in the study of the revisions which, as I say, is almost ready.

I have just one comment to make. Last year when the estimates of the Department of National Revenue were before the special committee on estimates I and

Dominion Succession Duty Act other members of that committee had an opportunity of going into this matter. I was rather hoping, as were one or two other members, that a remission would be made when a wife had contributed to the extent of one half of the estate. I realize that certain considerations would naturally have to be borne in mind by the minister before making any drastic change, even next fall, in the succession duty act, but I do feel he might consider taking at least one step in this direction at the present time, a step which, I think, would be quite logical.
I would like to point out that a great many Canadians, particularly new Canadians who are on farms, have wives who work in the fields and in the orchards just as hard as their husbands. This is the case in the tobacco industry and it is also true in certain other specialized branches of agriculture such as fruit growing and market gardening. I think some alteration in the act at the present time, before the new act comes out next fall, or whenever it does come out, would be very helpful in assisting in cases where a wife has in actual fact made a contribution during a lifetime of labour to the building up of the estate.
I repeat that there are specialized branches of agriculture in which, very often, some of our new citizens are employed where there is the sort of arrangement I have described. It would not be difficult for the act to be altered along these lines at the present time. The minister and his officials would then have more time in which to consider the more general plan of allowing all women to have the advantage of half the estate. As I say, I do think the widows of farmers- women who have actually contributed to the building up of an estate-should be the subject of special consideration at this time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the house will have noted the unanimity of the approval given to second reading of this bill by all parties in this house. It is significant that the proposal put forward by the government is one that, though we have debated it at the resolution stage, did not require to be debated today on second reading. However, before we proceed further with the discussion in the committee I think we should remind the minister of a few of the facts of life with regard to this whole matter.
As we have said on previous occasions, we welcome the steps now being taken by the government to put on our statute books a piece of legislation having to do with hospital insurance. Across the years we have contended that Canada should have at the federal level, in co-operation with the provinces, something more than hospital insurance. Indeed, it is our contention that we should have a broad, comprehensive program of health insurance. Nevertheless, this measure is a step in that direction and for that reason it is welcome.
I am reminded of the fact that in 1948, when Mr. King announced the health grants program, he stated amongst other things that the program was being initiated to lay the foundation for a nation-wide program of health insurance. I emphasize the point that on that occasion Mr. King did not make the suggestion that only hospital insurance was the goal. Rather he repeated what had been stated across the years, namely that the goal in this field is a nation-wide program of health insurance. In other words, it is our view that the day must come-and we feel that it should come soon-when we arrange for the payment of the medical bills of our people, including hospital, doctors, dentists, nurses and other care, on an insurance basis. As I say, it is because this bill is a step in that direction that we welcome it. It is because of that welcome that it has received the unanimous support of the house as indicated a few minutes ago.
We recognize the desirability of a program such as that envisaged in this bill being
Health Insurance
put on a joint federal-provincial basis. We go along with the minister in the statements he has made from time to time as to the desirability of the utmost of co-operation between the federal government and the provinces. It seems to us, though, that the federal government is not fully measuring up to its responsibility in the field of health insurance so far as the terms of this legislation are concerned.
We feel that the percentage of the cost of hospitalization to be paid by the federal government should be higher than the figure of roughly 50 per cent which is proposed under this bill. As I indicated at the resolution stage, we of the C.C.F. feel that that proportion should be 80 per cent. The reason that we contend that a larger proportion of the cost should be paid out of the moneys that Canadians pay in to the federal treasury is that the revenue of the federal treasury is collected more nearly on the basis of ability to pay than are the revenues of any other jurisdiction in this country.
We are not suggesting that hospital care can be had for nothing any more than any one would agree that free education is had for nothing. These things must be paid for. But what happens when you pay for them on a community or national basis is that you arrange for the payment on some other basis than that of the actual cost to each individual. Rather you arrange to pay for them on a social basis.
We have long since accepted the principle in this country that education is something that our people are entitled to regardless of the financial circumstances of the homes into which our children are born. I am sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare agrees with me that the day must come when we apply the same principle to hospital care and to health care across the board, that these are things to which our people are entitled and that therefore they should receive them not according to the length of one's purse but according to one's need for them.
As to paying for them, we should pay for them as we pay for other services that we recognize as being important to the community as a whole, namely on the basis of the ability to pay. It is for that reason that we contend that the proportion of hospital costs paid for by the federal government should be much higher than the 50 per cent set out in this bill. We say again, as we have

indicated at previous stages of this discussion -at the resolution stage and in questions on the orders of the day, and also in previous sessions-that the government in our view should include as shareable costs one or two items that are not yet included. I am thinking in particular of capital depreciation and one or two other items such as administrative costs.
We also feel that sufficient consideration has not yet been given to the claims of a number of the provinces that the care of tubercular patients and those who are mentally ill in hospitals should also be included in the plan. So long as you exclude those types of illness from the coverage provided in this bill it really works out that the federal government will be paying, not 50 per cent of the total hospital bills of the nation but rather some lesser figure, perhaps 30 per cent or 35 per cent at the most. We hope that even yet consideration will be given to extending the coverage under this bill to include these categories of illness.
I recognize the fact that once a government bill is in printed form the chances of getting many changes in a current session are not the best. But it is also our experience across the years that by hammering away at these things we get some ideas into the heads of hon. gentlemen opposite. The minister and all hon. members know that though we want to see this bill passed and put upon the statute books before this session ends, even if its ending is only a few days away, nevertheless by the terms of the bill it will not become effective for some months-perhaps a year and a half-after it is passed. In other words, there is time to reconsider the question of the cost of hospitalization of tubercular patients and those who are mentally ill.
We hope that in the interval between the date when this bill is passed and the time when it is put into effect in terms of the agreements being signed and payment made to the provinces that further consideration will be given to including these other types of illness.
We also press as strongly as we can, the point that the government should reconsider its formula concerning the time when payments under this bill will start. As the minister knows, when the Prime Minister made his statement in January 1956, the proposal was that this legislation would be introduced when a majority of the provinces representing a

majority of the population of Canada had indicated their agreement, and that it would be put into effect when that same number of provinces representing that same majority of the population of Canada had their plans in actual operation.

The original proposal was that no legislation would be even introduced into parliament until six provinces had agreed. is based on figures from the census of 1956. I submit that to insist that the population percentage should be any higher than that before further steps are taken is really ridiculous.

There has been one other change made with regard to the formula as to when the legislation will come into effect. We welcome this other change. It is that instead of the six provinces having to have their plans in actual operation it will be sufficient, according to the terms of this bill, if those provinces have their laws respecting their hospital plans in force. Provincial laws can come into force by virtue of a bill being assented to in the legislature or they can come into force by virtue of a proclamation. I believe that is an improvement over the former requirement that the six provinces had to have their plans in actual operation. I commend the government on the progress that it has made.
The government had taken a rather firm position and when the government takes a firm position, and particularly when it is hammered at by the opposition, it does not like to retreat from that position. The government has done so in these two respects; first, by introducing legislation when only five provinces have agreed and, secondly, by changing from the stipulation that plans must be in operation to the requirement that the appropriate provincial laws must be in force. I commend the government for what it has done.
I say to the government that, in all common sense, it ought to make this one further change. Surely, five provinces representing 56.3 per cent of the population of Canada are sufficient to get this great project launched. I hope consideration will be given to that point by the government while we are dealing with this bill. I emphasize that now because the requirement that a majority of the provinces representing a majority of the population in Canada have their plans enacted is written right into the bill itself. The minister knows that if the requirement for six provinces stays in the bill it will look as though that is the basis for still further delay in the actual coming into force of this plan. But if he were to change the bill to make five provinces sufficient bearing in mind the fact that five provinces, namely British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario and Newfoundland have agreed, then that element would be removed so far as the election campaign is concerned. It is not our intention to hold up this bill in any way. We have been in agreement so far as the bill is concerned. At the resolution stage, I pointed out certain things with which we were not in agreement. However, we do welcome this bill and we want to see it in operation. It is not our purpose, therefore, to hold up the bill by prolonged discussion. I intend to repeat some of the matters with which we are not in agreement. One of these is the question of depreciation. At the resolution stage I pointed out that depreciation should be allowed as a cost of these hospitals. I am aware of a hospital which lately wrote off some of their depreciation costs and this became a debt. Once this bill is passed, as I pointed out at the resolution stage, it is going to be very difficult for the organizations concerned with hospitals to go out to the public and seek donations, or try to raise money by the various means used by hospital committees.

Health Insurance
It is very apparent, and has been for years, that there is a need for a bill of this kind. I cited figures at the time of the resolution stage showing the high cost of hospitalization. The cost per patient per day, as I indicated at that time, has gone up from $7 and some odd cents to $14 and $15, a cost that makes it imperative that some measure of relief should be given to people who find it necessary to go to hospital. Such a cost is beyond the means of the average person in this country. When there is added to the cost of a severe illness, laboratory fees and fees for special nurses and the like, the fees of the medical man or the surgeon, sickness becomes a terribly expensive proposition.
I do draw your attention again to the fact that depreciation costs are something which should receive consideration in this bill on account of the difficulty of raising money, because the public feeling will be that once this bill is put through the federal or the provincial government in some way will be responsible for hospitals.
Another thing I do want to point out is that we should make very clear that this is a hospital insurance bill. Since the time that the resolution was brought in I have heard it discussed as health insurance. This is a hospital insurance bill.
The other matter that I brought up at the resolution stage was the question of tuberculosis and mental patients. It is true that tuberculosis is being well taken care of at the present time. Indeed the lists are going down. The number of cases is rapidly being reduced, and we are coming to a position that has not been common for a good many years. It is possible to get a patient into a sanitarium because we are arriving at the place where beds are available. That is owing to the fact that the measures which have been taken by the provincial departments of health, especially in Ontario, are cutting down the incidence of this disease year by year. The mass surveys conducted by the province have done a great deal in the cutting down of tuberculosis; but at the same time, those people who remain in hospitals are still hospital patients; they are still afflicted with an illness, sometimes a long-term illness. They are sick people. The same thing applies to mental diseases. There are some other things that I wish to say, in a consideration of mental disease, while we are on this bill.
In the estimates committee last year the minister gave his reasons for not recognizing mental disease. He agreed to accept mental disease while the individuals were patients in hospitals; that is, in the psychiatric wards of general hospitals; but his argument from there on was that mental disease patients, if accepted under this plan, would raise the cost

so that it would more or less defeat the plan and raise the cost of the insurance to the person wishing to obtain it. I point out to you, sir, that we have a problem in mental disease in Canada that we will have to cope with some place somehow. I do not like the fact that mental disease is not recognized because I feel it is a backward step. It is a backward step for this reason. Mental disease may occur just as you may have pneumonia or any other disease in the categories of diseases that are treated in hospitals at the present time.
The very fact that the statistics of Canada show there must be something done about this beyond the amounts that are given in the health grants for certain clinics and research proves my point. The number of people, as I pointed out the other day, suffering in mental hospitals is 10,000 more than the people who are occupying beds in all the other general hospitals put together. Something has to be done about this.
There was one bright spot brought out the other day. I noticed in statistics issued about a week ago that there were some signs of a letting-up of mental disease in Canada. We hope the percentages shown there will continue to grow, and that we may feel we are adequately dealing with this disease. We require more than what is laid down in the health grants for the treatment of mental disease.
I am sorry that some place in this bill the minister cannot go a step farther and give further financial help to the mental hospitals. It would be of great assistance. We need something more than the fact that under this scheme, when they are patients in general hospitals in this country, they qualify.
It is true that this bill is only the beginning. From time to time certain changes will be made in this legislation. I think that certain conditions laid down in the legislation at the present time may even have to be changed by legislation in the future. But in discussing this hospital situation, there is one point that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. He did not say it the other day when he was speaking on the resolution but I have noted his remarks in the press. I have read his speeches and I have heard him say that the health grants were responsible for the addition of 70,000 beds in Canada. May I say to the minister again, as I have said on previous occasions, and for the benefit of the committee, we ought to look at it in this way. Suppose we were building a hospital in the Ottawa valley-and I think the cost would run around $12,000 per bed-under the health grants the dominion government would give $1,000 for each new bed

and the province would give a matching grant. The donation of the federal government would be $1,000. If you took the $1,000 that is added by the province, and if the cost of the hospital bed in this year would be $12,000, it would leave $10,000. That money would have to be put up either by the municipality or by the various organizations interested in building hospital beds.
I feel very jealous on behalf of those people who have worked and are working to produce the $10,000. Therefore I think it is not altogether fair to say that the program has been responsible for 70,000 hospital beds. It is helping. Certainly, the assurance of $1,000 by the federal government and $1,000 by the provincial government is an incentive, but it is a long way from producing the 70,000 hospital beds.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre spoke of this as an election argument. I have said before in this house that in dealing with health I hope this matter will never become a political football. One must realize that every party in this house has been committed to some form of health or hospital insurance, and has been saying it over the years. I do not know how many speeches I have made on behalf of this party-the minister will agree with this-asking that something like this be done. I hope that when we go to the country we will not have any supporter of the government, any cabinet minister or anyone else, spreading his chest and saying, "I brought in health insurance". We have been asking for it; we want it. We are not going to delay this bill in spite of the fact we do think it has imperfections. We are going to vote for this bill. We want it passed and we want it passed as soon as possible.
The other day I brought in an amendment regarding the required six provinces and a majority of the people. The amendment was thrown out; it was not in order. We did express our opinion at that time regarding the number of provinces necessary to bring this bill into effect.
If this bill is necessary at the present time, if it is going to help people, let there be as little delay as possible. Again I point out it is not necessary to have the six provinces, or a majority of the people agreeing to it to bring it into effect.
Under these conditions the sooner we get this bill into operation in any province the better it will be. It is possible that when the bill is being discussed in the house we will make suggestions from time to time but we want to see this bill passed and the plan put in operation as soon as possible.

I see that the minister nods his head and I am sure he will do his best to see that this is done.
I suppose we all like to boast about our own provincial hospital scheme. My colleagues to my right frequently boast about the plan operating in Saskatchewan. That is perfectly all right and I think perhaps the people of Saskatchewan might think their plan is the best.
I am equally sure that the government of British Columbia feels that their plan is the best. The government in British Columbia, of course, inherited their hospitalization scheme. However, at the time they inherited it I think it can be said that the plan was in a terrible mess. It was based on the principle of the payment of premiums many of which had lapsed and the former government had a difficult time collecting premiums and making ends meet. A new government was elected there and they began to straighten out the complications of the scheme they inherited and I think today the people there are fairly well satisfied with it and perhaps think their plan is the best one.
Coming now to my own province of Alberta, we think we have a scheme which is the best. Because I come from that province I think I might be permitted to place on the

Health Insurance
record an outline of our scheme. The provincial government will enter into a contract with any municipality or city for the purpose of granting hospitalization to the citizens of Alberta at an extremely low rate. I think the rate throughout the province would presently average approximately $1.50 or $1.60 a day. Not many years ago it was known as the "dollar a day" hospitalization scheme. Of course, under the agreement that is struck with the municipalities the province gives grants under a certain formula and the municipalities make up the balance. They must include their contribution in the over-all municipal taxes they levy because they must get the money from some source.
If I may be permitted to cite a personal illustration I will tell you what happened in my own particular case. I took ill with sciatica in my left leg. I visited the doctor on a number of occasions and despite the fact that my leg was punctured with a needle a good many times the sciatica reached the point where I could not move. My wife said, "Well now, you have had it, I am going to call an ambulance." I was taken to the hospital in an ambulance and aside from the fact that I had sciatica there was nothing organically wrong with me and I was a hungry man.
I ate three square meals a day and I might say they were very good meals. Our local hospital is small but it is a highly efficient one. While there I received some shortwave treatments approximately every two or three days and I had a few small doses of medicine, a blood transfusion and an intravenous. I remained in the hospital for 30 days and on the thirtieth day I walked out and collected my bill at the desk. The total of my bill was exactly $30. I was very pleased at this and one cannot blame me if I walked out of the hospital feeling that we in Alberta had one of the best possible hospital schemes. In fact, I went home and in a jocular vein told my wife that I thought I would go back to the hospital because I could live there more cheaply than I could at home.
Of course, I did not get hospitalization for a dollar a day because there was an amount included in the annual tax bill on my home which represented my contribution to the scheme. However, I have my tax bill which I carry around in my brief case and the proportion of my taxes that went for hospitalization was $23.
One does not mind paying a little sum like that through taxes and one does not mind paying a moderate daily rate at the hospital either. It gives one an element of choice, a feeling that one is helping to pay for one's treatment. We in Alberta think we have one of the best hospitalization schemes.

I was in the hospital because of sciatica but they are able to give other patients much better treatment than that financially. The maternity cases are free; hospitalization is free; the old age pensioner accommodation is free and some other things of that nature.
Now I said that we would welcome the bill and the minister will not find opposition here in respect to it, but I would like to say something else and in so doing I do not want to say anything against the bill or the principle of hospitalization or insurance therefor. I do however believe that the government itself must look at these things in a much broader sense. I will pose this question: Why is it that hospitalization insurance schemes are necessary? Now the very moment I pose that question I think it is obvious that there can only be one answer to it and that is that the over-all picture shows that there are people in the country who cannot afford to pay for hospitalization.
We will grant that there will always be some people who cannot afford to pay their own hospital bills; that is natural. The poor are always with us, but I do believe that in the over-all picture the responsibility of the government is clear. I have said this before and I say it now, the best welfare state is a state where the income of all the people is sufficient for them to live on a very high standard of living where the production, not only of material wealth but of skills and services of the country, are at their disposal. In this way they are completely free to choose their own hospital, to choose their own doctor and to feel that they are financially able to take care of themselves when, unfortunate circumstances arise and they must be hospitalized. Now I think the responsibility of government must go that far and that is my main criticism of government policy on many other things as well as in matters of this kind.
There is one other point I would like to mention which was put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and that is that this issue may be kicked around in an election campaign. I do not know whether that would be so in his particular constituency or province or indeed in any other part of the country-perhaps it will be. I am going to say this, however, that I have passed through a good many elections personally and have fought quite a number of them but, do you know, the strange thing about it is that I have never fought a federal election when I have had to answer one question in respect to a national health or hospitalization scheme. Never have I been asked whether or not we support it; never

have I been asked whether or not the people can expect it. It may be that the people in my province and in my constituency are well satisfied with the scheme they have and therefore have no reason to ask the question.
However this does pose a question in my mind as to whether or not the people themselves really want it. From some quarters you would imagine that people would be clamouring for this thing; well, I do not know whether they are. I am not saying it is not a good thing, perhaps it is, but I have not personally witnessed any great clamour for it. I know there are organizations the officials of which will embody in their briefs certain proposals and urge the government to put in the plan because there are so many people who cannot afford hospitalization. Why can they not? That in my personal view is because there is something wrong somewhere else.
I do not think I need to say anything else along that line. The minister is going to receive our support and I do urge that the provinces should have every freedom. I will sit down now with just this last question to the minister so that when he gets up to reply to all he might answer whether or not the provinces who have agreed to come into this scheme-or all of them as far as that goes-have now seen this bill.

But I would like the opportunity of saying how disappointed I am that the government has seen fit to water down its original proposal of a comprehensive health insurance program to that of a program covering hospital care only.
I appreciate the argument that might be put forward by the minister, that this is part of an over-all program, but I think that the need in this country for a comprehensive scheme is so urgent at the present time that I do not think too many Canadians relish the idea of waiting as long for the next step as the period of time we have had to wait for this step to be taken.
I think that surveys have indicated that there is roughly twice as much being spent by the average Canadian on doctor bills, 82715-196J
Health Insurance
medical bills than on hospital bills, and consequently it would seem to me that the provision of some assistance in the field of medical care is long overdue.
I do not know when the government decided to stop talking in terms of health insurance and to emphasize the words "hospital care". This is of fairly recent origin. We used to hear speeches by supporters of the government referring to health insurance up until a few years ago and then gradually it has been a watering down process. Now I am sure that just as we are not satisfied that the legislation has gone far enough there are other groups in the country who are equally as dissatisfied. The Canadian Labour Congress in its submission to the federal cabinet made rather specific recommendations regarding health insurance and pointed out that health insurance should have the highest priority and that there should be an early implementation of a nation-wide program of health care.
You will note that they did not merely ask for hospitalization. They asked for something which has been promised for many years. They asked for over-all health care. They went on to point out that this should include preventive, diagnostic, curative and rehabilitation service rendered by physicians, dentists, surgeons and other health agencies. They recommended that such a comprehensive program should be initiated on a nation wide basis either by the government of Canada or jointly in co-operation with the provinces as a complete health insurance plan.
The step taken by the government of Canada in offering to pay a share of the cost of hospital care in the six provinces is worthy of commendation. It is a move in the right direction, but the Canadian Labour Congress does not take the view that a comprehensive nation wide health insurance plan cannot be implemented without further delay. The last sentence in these recommendations outlines their position quite clearly-that while they agree with the proposals advanced by the government as far as they go, the Canadian Labour Congress is not satisfied that the government has gone as far as it could go at the present time.
There are a number of other shortcomings in the legislation. I was rather disappointed in the comments made by the minister when he introduced this legislation at the resolution stage, and turned his thumbs down on what I thought was a reasonable proposal that the federal government should be prepared to provide for the care of those who are in mental hospitals and t.b. sanatoria. The fact that some of the provincial governments have undertaken to provide full care is no reason why this should be used as an excuse

Health Insurance
to the disadvantage of the provinces. It is no reason why the federal government should discriminate against such provinces with respect to the care of patients in mental hospitals or in t.b. sanatoria.
I agree with our mental health officials who say that one of the most important things we must do is eliminate the artificial distinction between illness of what might be called a physical nature on one hand, and illness of a mental nature on the other. We must erase from the public mind the attitude that there is something different between a patient who is in a mental hospital and one who is in an ordinary general hospital. I think we could go a long way toward doing that if we included all sick people who require hospitalization	within the	scope	of	this
legislation.
The government has not	seen fit to do
this, yet statistics reveal that a very high percentage of	hospitalized	people	in	this
country are in mental institutions.
I think the government should be prepared to go a long way in an effort to build up a better attitude of mind among the general public with regard to mental illness. One way of doing	that would	be, as	I	have
suggested, to include all hospital patients within one over-all hospitalization scheme.
It seems to me, that there are a number of other grave shortcomings in the legislation. Some of them have been noticed by newspapers which normally support the government. I have here a copy of an editorial from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of March 29 of this year entitled: "Two Glaring Omissions" and it has to do with this present measure. The editorial states, among other things:
One matter in particular has not attracted the public attention we think it deserves. We refer to the federal government's omission of two legitimate and familiar expense items from the list of shareable hospital costs on which calculations of Ottawa's proposed contributions to provincial plans depend. These two items are annual depreciation charges and annual interest charges on capital debt. Depreciation charges are the amounts set aside each year by a hospital for the day when expensive renovation and expansion programs will have to be undertaken. Interest charges are the annual payments an institution must make on outstanding capital debt.
Ottawa ignores both these cost items in calculating per capita hospitalization costs. As a result its percapita cost figures do not give a true account of the operating costs of the nation's hospitals. Consequently, Ottawa will not be contributing an average "50 per cent towards the national cost of standard public ward care and the normal services that go with it," as health minister Martin is so fond of saying.
I think it is significant that this quite valid criticism of the legislation should come from a newspaper which over the years has consistently supported the Liberal party. I was

not too greatly impressed by the minister's presentation when he introduced this measure, because it seems to me that after many years of waiting the minister sought to take too much credit for himself and for the government for having at last brought forth a part of a program, a program which should have been instituted a great many years ago.
I know that before the last general election whenever we raised the question of health insurance we were told, in my constituency at least, that we already had a health insurance program. The rather tortuous argument was used that since some of the grants had been provided by the government, that because this amounted to, perhaps, one-twentieth of a program, that constituted a health insurance scheme. I think the man in the street is not going to judge a program on that basis. He is going to look for results, and I think we have long passed the time when we can allow this business to continue as it has done in the past.
Good health is essential to the nation's well-being, and a comprehensive health insurance plan should not be measured merely in terms of dollars and cents. The amount of money which it is going to cost should be considered in terms of how the expenditure will affect the well-being of the Canadian people. I think it is shortsighted to take the attitude that we must regard this program merely in terms of money spent.
There are a number of other matters I would like to mention at this time but it is not my intention to hold up the legislation. I want to see it go through and I want to see my own province in a position where it can apply for and obtain some benefit from the measure now before us.
Reference has been made to the hospitalization programs in the various provinces. As a citizen of Saskatchewan, I want to say that I have always been proud of our own scheme. I am very proud of the fact that Saskatchewan has pioneered in this field, and I think the hospitalization legislation brought in by the C.C.F. government immediately after that government went into office has set the pace for other provinces. As is well known, several other provinces have followed suit.

adjournment time I had this hospital bill in a state of intangibility, and now probably I should bring it into tangible form. Prior to the recess I had mentioned the long time it had taken this government to introduce this health plan. In fact, however, it is not a health plan, as I stated, because it has now evolved into a hospitalization plan. Time after time during election campaigns this health plan has been held out as an alluring proposition by the government in order to aid its return to office. I might say that many times it accomplished its purpose.
The plan had been forgotten in the early years. They said it was going to cost a considerable amount of money to introduce it. During some election campaigns the Conservative party was upbraided because they said it was going to be very costly. We were accused of trying to frustrate the plan because of the cost. Gradually the government came around to the idea that it was going to cost quite a bit. The people became tired of waiting for this plan. Medical costs and hospital costs began to mount. During the war these costs became prohibitive; the people could not afford them. They took matters into their own hands and got insurance of their own which would help them stand the strain of long illnesses in their families. Then these hospital plans became quite the fashion and there were various plans by which people were able to insure themselves against hospital costs. This caused a great demand to be made upon hospital accommodation.
It was just about that time the war started and the hospitals were subjected to the extra burden of war casualties being returned to Canada. The government was hard pressed to find accommodation. I know that the government did grant sufficient money to help build a wing on the Toronto East general hospital, which is adjacent to my riding, in order to take care of the soldiers. I am sure the same thing was done for other hospitals. After the war was over there was
TMr. Small.]
an increased number of beds available, but even that did not meet the demand for hospital beds.
The demand for hospital plans continued at such a rate that the provinces themselves had to do something about it. The provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan adopted their own hospital plan. These provinces gained a lot of experience and found what it costs to run hospitals. One after another the provinces entertained the idea that they should have such plans. In fact, the adoption of health plans continued at such a tempo the federal government was afraid it would be faced with such a hodgepodge of medical care plans in the provinces that the dominion government would not be able to introduce its own plans.
Then confronted with this phenomenal expansion in hospitals the Ontario government came up with their per bed allowance of $1,000 to aid hospital construction. The federal government matched this allowance, some two years later. The dominion government then came up with what I term their Rip Van Winkle plan. After sleeping for nearly 40 years they introduced a plan at the dominion provincial conference. The conditions that were set out as the prerequisites for the implementation of the plan, such as the six provinces having to participate, and the insufficiency of the federal government contributions were not acceptable so the Ontario government objected. It was stated that 50 per cent of the people would have to enter such a plan. The provinces said they could not meet these conditions. Then it began to dawn upon them that perhaps these conditions had been submitted for bargaining purposes or for the purpose of delaying the introduction of the government's health plan. However, later the number of people needed to make this plan work was agreed upon and the provinces indicated their agreement, so these impediments to the adoption of the plan were removed.
Last year, after the plan had been submitted, we heard from Ontario, through its premier, that Ontario had some objections. What then was the province of Ontario going to do? Because the province would not accept the federal plan holus-bolus it was placed in the light of frustrating the government's plans. The truth of the matter is that Ontario had always been in favour of having a national health plan. The people of that province could see that such a plan was necessary in this country, but this government was reluctant to move. Time after time in the house you could hear them say, "What is Ontario going to do about this?" This plan could not work under the conditions set down

by the federal government unless Ontario was in it. Quebec, for reasons best known to itself, is not going to participate in it and Ontario is the only other province with a population large enough to make this plan work. If Ontario were taken out of the picture, all the other provinces from coast to coast could not operate it. It was, therefore, necessary to have Ontario in the plan.
They started to bargain, and I will say that there were compromises made on both sides. The premier of Ontario, in a spirit of compromise and a desire to see this plan work, gave some very vital concessions. If this plan is adopted, and I hope it will be, it will be as the result of one thing; I want the members on the government side of the house to understand this. If this bill goes through and the plan is put in force, it will be as a result of one thing and that is that the premier of Ontario made concessions in order that we would have this plan.

I had hoped that not only a hospital insurance scheme but a health insurance scheme would soon be part of the statutes of the Dominion of Canada. We are glad that this legislation has finally come to the house and is to be enacted. We only question why it was that the government waited so long, and why it was that they waited just three months before a general election to bring the legislation before the house. One can only conclude, perhaps, that the political side of the question was more in the mind of the minister and the government than the health problem.
There is one very serious fault with this legislation, which I am sure is going to be aired by those who speak on behalf of a great number of people in Canada. I refer particularly to the mentally ill. This legislation should include all persons who are sick.
Health Insurance
I suggest to the minister that some day Canada will have insurance legislation which will cover everyone who is ill. To discriminate in this way is a very serious thing for a large number of people in Canada who become ill. It is the very type of discrimination which is bad in all kinds of illness; it suggests segregation.
Experiments and practice have shown- and I recommend to the minister that he study what the government of Saskatchewan has done in the way of treatment of the mentally ill-that much can be done for the mentally ill. The progress made in Saskatchewan has shown that where adequate staff and modern facilities are provided about 85 per cent of the people who become mentally ill can be returned to their homes as useful citizens. That is a great revelation. The terrible record of the mentally ill in this country, the treatment of them in the past, is really a condemnation, when proper treatment and facilities could have cured so many. We now know that 85 per cent of those who become mentally ill can be returned to a useful life merely by the provision of adequate staff, modern facilities and modern practice. When we think of that, why should we discriminate against them in legislation such as this?
In his statement to the house I hope the minister will explain exactly what will be done, because those who are excluded under this legislation are those who suffer from tuberculosis in sanitaria, and also those who are mentally ill in mental institutions. What about the hospital which has one wing in which psychiatric patients are treated? That type of hospital and that type of treatment are really the best. That is the kind of treatment which has been found to be one of the important factors in recovery.
I had the rather fortunate experience of being a patient in the university hospital in Saskatoon last fall for nine or ten days with a gallstone operation. I had the opportunity to see what they were doing there, where the facilities were so good, where the staff was adequate and where the medical staff could be interchanged with those of the psychiatric ward. The records of recovery in that institution are an indication that this kind of legislation is much too slow and much too late. Surely if our object is to keep in step with the advances that are being made today, to keep in step with what scientific knowledge demands as being important, why should the present government, which the Minister of National Health and Welfare is so ready to praise as always in the forefront, always being in the advance -and we listen to it daily-be so slow and so hesitant in this case?

Health Insurance
I plead with him to reconsider the exclusion of the tubercular and mentally ill patients. The Canadian mental health association refers to this as being a most vicious and most immoral type of discrimination against the sick, and particularly against helpless people, 85 per cent of whom could be restored if adequate help were provided. I am sure that on the very grounds of economy it would be good to include these people in this insurance plan. In the end it would be cheaper; in the end it would be more effective and it would save thousands of good Canadians, who are today in fairly good health, from being condemned to a life of uselessness and misery in the type of institutions which are a disgrace to any nation which considers it is in the forefront and a leader in the treatment of the ill.
I give the minister those thoughts and I say to him that I shall have more to say when we come to the clauses of the bill. I conclude by saying I hope the minister will make a statement to the house when we are discussing the clauses of the bill, indicating the readiness of the government to go forward. Perhaps he would indicate also some of the latest figures that his research department has with regard to the cures that are being effected among the mentally ill of Canada. He might also give some of the figures that have been revealed in this country of the large increase in the number of people who are becoming mentally ill. It is a major problem in our country.
I am not saying that the government has done nothing. The people have been glad to receive the grants from the federal government for the treatment of the mentally ill; but here is a chance to do something progressive. I think it is a terrible flaw in this legislation to exclude the tubercular and mentally ill people. It means segregation, which is the very opposite of what it should do.
