Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that I will not prolong this debate more than three or four minutes.
I have no intention of opposing the adoption of the hospital insurance proposition which is now before the committee and which was given so quickly second reading this afternoon. State assistance is obviously indispensable to hospitalization and research services for poorer patients. Going even further I

might add that, according to the terms of this present plan, medical costs themselves should be included. For a number of reasons, medical costs, and especially hospital costs have reached a prohibitive level for people of low income. None the less, if there is one thing which concerns the individual personally and engages his full responsibility, it is indeed his health and the means of maintaining it or recovering it if it has been impaired. The responsibility of the state in that field, as in that of education for instance, can only be complementary. I therefore feel certain misgivings about the interference of the state, whether federal or provincial, in a field which concerns the personal life of the individual.
I have already dealt with that question here more than once and at some length. I might merely add today that citizens conscious of their own responsibility could very well leave it to private companies to carry the financial risks of illness that will befall the individual, often at some unexpected moment of his life. I refer of course to insurance companies and to health insurance companies operated on the principle of mutual benefit. Quite clearly, on the other hand, many people of low income cannot afford the premium charged by those companies to cover the care to individuals, and particularly to families. It is then that the government must step into the picture and play the complementary part 1 have just mentioned, by assuming the cost of this premium. In that way, the individual and the family keep their independence and full freedom.
It may be objected that insurance companies might take undue advantage of the situation. That is possible; but then it would again be a government responsibility to safeguard public interest and investigate to uncover and repress any such abuses.
Then too, the complementary part of the state should belong to the provinces, and not to the central government. I will not labour the point, because my views are well known here, as well as in the riding I represent.
However, since a majority of the provinces seem to prefer sharing their responsibilities with the central government in that field, I do not see why the federal government should not seek a way of meeting the request of the province of Quebec particularly, since a great majority of its taxpayers do share, I think, my humble opinion on that matter.

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the government for bringing forward this bill, a bill by which they can pay a great share of the national hospital insurance costs. I feel that the necessary six provinces will come into this scheme and that this will eliminate once and for all the fear and the dread which our people have of high hospital expenses. Such bills are often contracted at a time when people are getting along in life and their earning power is small. I understand that the bill will provide for one-half of the cost of ordinary sicknesses and non-compensatory accidents, as well as one-half of the cost of the diagnostic procedures incidental to good medical and surgical treatment.
In looking over section 4, and I may be a little out of order here, I do think this section contains a most ingenious formula. I think it tends to keep down the high cost of hospitalization in the high-cost provinces and that it will also tend to increase the standard of hospital treatment in the low-cost provinces. Furthermore it provides a mathematical control only, and I think this is very important because otherwise we would have direct interference on the part of the Department of National Health and Welfare in matters which come under provincial jurisdiction.
Each province has to bear the cost of administration. Now I think this is wise particularly since, as there are different collection costs in each of the different provinces, it would not be fair for one province to be raising money by taxation and another by premiums, for example. I can conceive of no better scheme; I think it is most generous to the provinces and I feel sure the people will take it up very readily.
I believe further that the national health insurance scheme would be difficult of attainment without the national health program which has been in vogue for nine years in Canada. We have spent something over $220 million; we have provided or helped to provide many hospital beds in new hospitals and in hospital extensions; we have spent much money on the control of diseases such as tuberculosis, venereal diseases, cancer and have also spent much money in the training of professional people. One recent

example of such spending which has turned out very well indeed was given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare when he reported not long ago on the results of the immunization against polio in Canada. The preliminary reports for 1956 showed that the incidence of polio was only 15 per cent of the last five year average and that only ten cases of paralysis occurred where the victim had received vaccination and no cases of paralysis had occurred in cases where the full complement of three doses had been given.
We have spent $3 million on this service and this will be returned to us many fold, not only in that we will not have handicapped children but also that we will not have them in hospitals for long periods undergoing remedial surgery.
There are many features in this hospital plan that I like very much, particularly the fact that it is going to be available to all. I would like the compulsory feature since all Canadians will be paying into this scheme in their federal taxes. There is no time limit as to hospitalization and we know that in certain very severe accidents involving multiple fractures and in terminal illnesses people are often in hospital much longer than they could be under the present insurance schemes now in vogue and still have their bills paid for them.
Hospitals should be able to budget and not have large deficits; they should be able to get away from the different drives that are put on to raise money to cover these deficits.
Furthermore there will now be no exclusions. I have had patients in hospital recovering from surgery, for example, who have looked over their policy and found that they have been excluded, particularly when they read the fine print in the policy. This puts me in mind of an Amos and Andy story, where Andy had had his taxicab smashed up in an automobile accident and he went down to collect his insurance and his attention was called to the fine print. Someone produced a magnifying glass and he said that he had been magnified right out of his insurance.
Now I do know that most insurance companies have provided good protection, but certainly some other insurance companies have sold cheap policies and people have not been able to collect when they needed the money.
I think one point was missed in discussing the different pensions which have been brought before the house recently in connection with the budget and that is that the municipalities and provinces will be saved a great deal of money when this bill comes into effect. A great number of our civil pensioners, old age pensioners and those who

come under the Old Age Assistance Act, blind pensioners and disabled pensioners, when they go into hospital, become direct charges on the provinces and on the municipalities for their hospitalization. Now in the future if the provinces assume their half of the cost and the dominion assumes its part, the municipalities will be relieved completely from this indigent cost. If on the other hand these costs are carried forward in the same proportion that they are carried forward today, the municipalities will have very much less to pay.
I am often asked what this plan might be expected to cost and that is a very hard thing to say, but I think the cost should be very moderate unless the provinces-any of the provinces-decide to include in their hospitalization bills the tubercular and mental hospitalization costs, which naturally would be different in each province.
Then they would not need to take that money to run these hospitals out of consolidated revenue. In my opinion this is a great humanitarian act on the part of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Prime Minister and of this government. The one feature about this bill which appeals to me most is the fact that it makes hospitalization available to all, rich and poor alike.

I wonder whether a specialized clinic or a hospital privately owned would be included under the act. At the moment I am thinking of something in the line of the Banff arthritis clinic.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: If it is licensed by the province as a hospital it could be so regarded.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Is a nursing home licensed by the province a hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Yes, it is a hospital if it is licensed by the province. If a nursing home is licensed by the province, it is a hospital for the purposes of this act.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: A nursing home becomes a hospital if it is licensed by the province and therefore is eligible?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: On that same point may I ask this question? I have not heard the entire discussion. In Ontario private hospitals licensed by the province would be eligible but it does not say for public ward cases. I assume that under the arrangement public ward rates would be paid to the private hospitals.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Public ward rates.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENTS FROM CONSOLIDATED REVENUE FUND
speechtext: Public ward rates for the care of patients. The thing that bothers me about private hospitals-and there are some very good private hospitals, as the minister knows-is that no element of the cost takes into account the provision of their buildings and the maintenance of them. Is there any possibility of a different arrangement for private hospitals which do not receive funds from this government or from the provincial government to maintain their building at their expense?
